projects.title: Quantum Optimization Algorithm To Efficiently Route Public Transportation In Cities
projects.description: Cars are one of the biggest polluters of greenhouse gases and to reduce their impact on the environment, there needs to be a nation-wide shift towards the use of public transportation - specifically the use of buses. Designing new bus routes can help buses arrive more frequently on time, especially during rush hour, which is an incentive for people to use buses. The Urban Transit Routing Problem (UTRP) is an NP-hard optimization problem, solved with heuristic algorithms that output approximate solutions, that focuses on constructing bus routes from an existing road network. The purpose of this project is to use quantum computing to solve the UTRP by minimizing a road network’s average travel time (ATT), a measure of the average travel time for all passengers to travel between all pairs of bus stops. My engineering goal was to use quantum computing, which has a theoretical advantage over heuristics in solving NP-hard problems, to produce routes with a lower ATT than heuristics for Mandl’s Swiss benchmark and existing bus routes in downtown Seattle. My algorithm achieved an ATT of 10.11 minutes for the benchmark, which is an improvement over current UTRP solvers. Additionally, my algorithm decreased the ATT in a section of downtown Seattle by 53%. This research supported my engineering goals by showing the feasibility of using quantum computers to develop routes with a lower ATT than both classical heuristic methods for a benchmark and existing bus routes in downtown Seattle.

activity.title: A draft of my blog post on combinatorial optimization problems and potential quantum computing solutions in the pharmaceutical industry is now on the Iff.bio website - https://iff.bio/blog.html . I describe the drug-discovery pipeline, and the various tracks of getting a compound to market, and talk about classical and quantum algorithms for molecular docking, clinical trial design, supply chain optimization, and the dynamic filling drug optimization problem. I focused on problems that quantum algorithms and QPU's could potentially provide a speedup for over classical solutions. Thank you so much to Samarth Sandeep and Kirk McGregor for their guidance and help throughout writing this blog post, and I’m looking forward to working more on using quantum computing for Molecular Docking and learning more about pharma-related combinatorial optimization problems! ...more

It was a great week at the IEEE World Congress on SERVICES 2026 in Sydney earlier this July, and I'm still thinking about the insightful conversations. I had the honour of giving an invited talk at the IEEE Quantum Software 2026 Symposium: "When Quantum Meets AI in the Cloud: A Software Systems Perspective on Resource Orchestration." My argument was simple: Quantum advantage will not arrive through hardware advancement alone. It will also depend on the quantum software systems and cloud services that decide what runs where, when, and at what cost. That layer still feels wide open to me, and it may be where our community can move most quickly. Two of our papers at the congress approach that problem from different ends: - QBugLM (IEEE QSW 2026) starts with the developer, asking whether LLM agents can genuinely debug quantum programs. We give the community an agentic benchmark framework to measure what these agents can actually do in finding and repairing bugs for quantum software. - QCOEM (IEEE CLOUD 2026) starts with the platform, treating quantum cloud orchestration as a multi-objective problem where fidelity, waiting time, and cost rarely agree. Here we solve those trade-offs with evolutionary optimisation, which complements the deep reinforcement learning angle we took earlier in DRLQ and QFOR. Both point toward what we are building at QuantumAI.Cloud (QAC) intersection: quantum as a cloud resource, and AI as the layer that helps developers and orchestrators reason about it. 🎉 Huge thanks to the organisers, my supervisor Muhammad Usman , my co-authors and students Tam Pham and Andrew Pham , who together did the great work. Still early days for us at QAC, but that is exactly what makes it worth doing. #QAC #QuantumSoftware #QuantumCloud #QBugLM #QCOEM

Some people see business travel and think, “That must be nice.” What they don’t see are the 5:00 a.m. departures, working from hotel rooms, customer dinners, long days, and the work waiting the moment you get home. I left Tuesday morning at 5:00 a.m., flew to Nebraska, went straight to the hotel, and got to work. That evening I met with a couple of potential clients over dinner, and the next day I had the opportunity to build relationships at the Cornhusker Classic. Now it’s 5:00 a.m. CST, and I’m on my way back to Las Vegas. As soon as I land, I’m jumping straight into six back to back meetings. The grind creates the opportunity. Every early flight, every customer conversation, every mile traveled, and every meeting is another chance to earn trust, solve problems, and help others succeed. I’m grateful to be part of the team at Bild AI that’s building something special, and I’m excited for what’s ahead.

It was truly a pleasure, I got all sorts of interesting questions from "What is a quantum computer, really?" to questions about me personally, like "Do you still see building a seawater powered car as viable?" Always a good time with students and an even better time at Aggie Square :)

Last week, I walked the stage at the University of Washington ’s commencement ceremony. As I stood there, I thought about how different my journey ended up being from what I originally expected. When I started studying computer science, I never imagined I would complete my degree two years early and head directly into a full time role at Amazon . But looking back, what stands out most isn’t any single achievement. Over the past two years, I completed my private pilot flight training, competed nationally on a Bollywood fusion dance team, founded and grew UW’s intercollegiate competitive cricket club, and contributed to research at the Programmable Matter Lab. What connected all of these experiences wasn’t a master plan but a mindset of growth and learning. I’ve realized that some of the most meaningful opportunities in college (and in life) come from saying yes to things before you feel fully qualified for them. Joining a dance workshop. Taking on a challenging course load. Starting an organization that didn’t exist. Exploring a field you know little about. Many of the skills and opportunities that shaped my journey came from pursuing interests that initially had nothing to do with my career, and developing those skills through various learning experiences. For students and early-career professionals, my biggest takeaway is this: Your growth is often determined less by the opportunities available to you and more by your willingness to step into unfamiliar situations and learn. The people who grow the fastest aren’t always the ones with the clearest roadmap. They’re the ones who stay curious, keep showing up, and consistently put themselves in environments where they can learn. I’m incredibly grateful to my family, friends, peers, and professors who challenged me, supported me, and helped me grow along the way. This July, I’ll be starting my full-time role at Amazon. I’m excited for the next chapter and, more importantly, for all the new things I’ll get to learn. Here’s to staying curious. #UniversityOfWashington #UWAlumni #ComputerScience #TechCareers #Amazon #ContinuousLearning #GrowthMindset #SoftwareEngineering #Innovation
